Register Paper locations have been assigned, authors can now register: Author Registration Information Paper presentation preferences emails to Authors have been sent, responses are due by Sept. 30 AOE The Career site is open See this blog post for details on the registration process Aug 25, 2026: NeurIPS has no affiliation or partnership with any third-party service that claims to collect registration or housing information on our behalf. The only authorized source for NeurIPS registration and Housing is through the official NeurIPS website. Please do not share registration details with any outside party. July 23, 2026: Due to a technical issue during release, we are currently re-releasing all reviews and initial meta-reviews. Reviews will be temporarily offline during that time. AI Reviewing Experiment This year NeurIPS will be held in Sydney, Atlanta, and Paris. Author Eligibility. We want to speak directly to the concern many of you have expressed, and we owe you a clear explanation of what happened, why it happened, and where we stand now. We understand this situation caused genuine alarm and we take that seriously. In preparing the NeurIPS 2026 handbook, we included a link to a US government sanctions tool that covers a significantly broader set of restrictions than those NeurIPS is actually required to follow. This error was due to miscommunication between the NeurIPS Foundation and our legal team; there was never an intention to restrict participation beyond our mandatory compliance obligations. The responsibility for that error is ours as an organization, and we deeply apologize for the alarm and impact this miscommunication had on our community. We have updated the link and clarified the text of our policy, which is consistent with that of ACM and IEEE, as well as other international conferences and NeurIPS in the past. As in previous years, NeurIPS welcomes submissions from all compliant institutions and individuals. We want to reiterate that NeurIPS is a community-driven event, created by and for the community, and strives to be inclusive. The NeurIPS 2026 organizing committee was particularly saddened to learn of this institutional miscommunication. The organizing committee has taken on the responsibility of running the conference this year with the goal of fostering open communication, knowledge sharing, and global scientific discourse. We thank the community for bringing this issue to our attention and working with us through this situation. Santos University of Amsterdam Mission Statement The Neural Information Processing Systems Foundation is a non-profit corporation whose purpose is to foster the exchange of research advances in Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning, principally by hosting an annual interdisciplinary academic conference with the highest ethical standards for a diverse and inclusive community. About the Conference The conference was founded in 1987 and is now a multi-track interdisciplinary annual meeting that includes invited talks, demonstrations, symposia, and oral and poster presentations of refereed papers. Along with the conference is a professional exposition focusing on machine learning in practice, a series of tutorials, and topical workshops that provide a less formal setting for the exchange of ideas. items.title: Flint-interactive: A language for creating interactive data visualizations
items.summary: At a glance Brings rich interactivity to AI-generated charts: Flint-interactive enables agents to create data visualizations that users can explore directly through clicking, filtering, zooming, highlighting, and cross-chart interactions. Makes complex interactions easier to build: Instead of requiring low-level visualization code, Flint-interactive lets users and agents define behaviors using high-level semantic events and update operators. Improves reliability and reduces development effort: By using Flint’s compiler to handle interaction logic and visual dependencies, the system helps avoid many of the layout, rendering, and debugging challenges common in custom interactive visualizations. Connects charts, text, tables, and applications: Flint-interactive supports interactive data stories, dashboards, and connected experiences where actions in one view can update charts, documents, widgets, or application state in another. AI agents make it easy to analyze data and generate reports
items.content: At a glance Brings rich interactivity to AI-generated charts: Flint-interactive enables agents to create data visualizations that users can explore directly through clicking, filtering, zooming, highlighting, and cross-chart interactions. Makes complex interactions easier to build: Instead of requiring low-level visualization code, Flint-interactive lets users and agents define behaviors using high-level semantic events and update operators. Improves reliability and reduces development effort: By using Flint’s compiler to handle interaction logic and visual dependencies, the system helps avoid many of the layout, rendering, and debugging challenges common in custom interactive visualizations. Connects charts, text, tables, and applications: Flint-interactive supports interactive data stories, dashboards, and connected experiences where actions in one view can update charts, documents, widgets, or application state in another. AI agents make it easy to analyze data and generate reports with data visualizations. They help users examine patterns more efficiently than by reading verbose text. However, when we’re feeling exploratory, we want to go beyond static visualizations. : We want to interact with charts to zoom in on details, compare data across charts, or even highlight related text in the document from a chart selection, and vice versa. This requires agents to be able to create interactive data visualizations that communicate information while letting readers explore beyond the author’s chosen view, ideally with the quality of interactive stories in sophisticated data journalism. This leaves us wondering: (As a user) Can I interact with charts directly in chat to explore the data and ask follow-up questions based on what I select? (As a developer) Can I enable the AI agents I build for my customers to generate interactive visualizations that help them explore and understand their data? Yes, it’s possible, but there is a significant practical gap. Even with capable frontier models, we still face: High generation cost. Agents rarely produce a fully satisfactory interactive visualization in one turn. Repeated rounds of reasoning, coding, and debugging consume tokens and time. Reliability. Interactive visualizations are challenging enough that expressive interactive charts introduce poor layouts or broken interactions easily, and we risk introducing new problems when trying to fix them. These challenges help explain why consistently generating high-quality interactive visualizations remain difficult in real-world use. Meanwhile, built-in interactions in some visualization libraries are not expressive enough on their own to create bespoke interactive charts. And these challenges are results of the lack of an expressive yet high-level language to specify visual interactions. Microsoft Research StorY OptiMind: When the system meets the floor A three‑month pilot in a Midwestern bottling plant shows what happens when AI moves beyond chat and into decision-making, where constraints shift, stakes are real, and answers must hold. Learn more Opens in a new tab Flint-interactive Flint-interactive (opens in new tab) is a language for creating interactive data visualizations on top of Flint. It allows users to create dashboards, data stories, and interactive artifacts more easily. The power of Flint-interactive comes from Flint’s compiler, which translates user interactions into semantic events that capture the meaning behind what users select. It then uses high-level operators to update visualizations in response to those events, making sophisticated interactions far easier to create and maintain. This shifts the heavy burden of resolving complex dependencies between interaction and visual logic to the compiler, so the user (or the agent) can easily describe expressive interactions with high-level specifications. Example 1: We can enable the user to brush one visual view, and the chart highlights all groups of country selected by the user with a simple preset interaction linked-brush. How to use 1. Use Flint in your chat Use Flint Interactive directly in your chat or canvas environment through Flint-MCP and MCP Apps, following the MCP setup guide. With the latest release, tell your agent what to chart and which interactions you want; it can generate an interaction_spec alongside the Flint chart spec and render the interactive chart in your conversation. Example 2: Using Flint-interactive in the chat environment, allowing the agent to produce interactive charts more reliably with simple Flint specifications. It also enables the user to select and pass context to the follow-up turns. 2. Build an interactive app with Flint Build interactive charts in a dashboard, data story, or other application with Flint Interactive Canvas. Your app can use event handlers to process semantic events emitted by Flint Canvas, for example to filter a table, update another chart, or change application state. To let your app’s widgets control how the chart updates, send update operators to Flint Canvas. Example 2: Flint-interactive allows developers to define interactions between charts and external elements (e.g., table, paragraph). Here, the user can click the table to highlight points in the chart and verse versa. 3. Create bespoke interactions To create bespoke interactions beyond Flint’s presets, define a trigger and a custom handle function with the programming API that maps semantic events to custom chart update sequences. For example, a handler can highlight a clicked country and label it by name. It combines set-style and set-annotation without manipulating renderer-specific marks. Example 4: The agent can create bespoke interactive visualizations with Flint’s programming API. In this DimpVis example, the user can drag the point along the time path to visualize how all cities’ temperature and precipitation changes. How it works Flint Canvas is a state machine that tracks user interactions on the canvas and manages visual rendering state. Flint makes interaction specification easy by separating visual logic, managed by the compiler, from interaction logic, specified by the user at the semantic level: Visual logic: The compiler automatically resolves raw triggers, such as clicks, drags, and key presses, into semantic events that identify chart elements and data. It also translates update operators into rendered canvas changes, handling hit testing, and low-level visual updates. Interaction logic: The user specifies interactions by mapping semantic interaction events to chart update operators, such as set style to highlight data, set annotation to label a point, or set viewport to pan or zoom. The user can also use those semantic events to update external tables, widgets, or application states. Figure 1: Flint interactive allows the agent to describe interaction logic by mapping “what semantic event is the user interacting with” to “what updates they want for the canvas surface”. The compiler takes the heavy lifting of resolving visual updates and manages the runtime, which makes interaction authoring more reliable c and cost effective. This separation means users do not need to reverse-engineer rendering logic or manipulate renderer-specific marks, making interactions easier to specify and maintain. Furthermore, because event generation and visual updates are compositional, the same model also connects Flint with tables, text, other charts, and widgets to build interactive stories and dashboards. Try it now! Video playback requires cookie consent Chart users: Set up Flint in your chat (opens in new tab) and ask your agent to create an interactive chart. Find inspiration in the interaction gallery. App builders: Build interactive dashboards, data stories, and connected views with the programming API (opens in new tab) . Share the interaction-author skill with your coding agent to add presets to your app. Interaction designers: Explore the bespoke examples (opens in new tab) , design a new interaction, and turn it into a reusable preset. Propose a preset on GitHub and share your prototype or implementation to help expand Flint’s interaction vocabulary. items.content: At a glance Formal methods for everyday software. PDD Kit helps you turn your intent into a formal spec, then proves the code your agent writes for every input and uses tests where a proof can’t reach. It takes formal methods beyond niche, specialist work to engineers without a formal methods background and to everyday applications, like the full-stack web app shown here. Exhaustive line-by-line human review can become difficult to scale as AI agents generate increasingly large amounts of code. The plan is supposed to be the contract between you and a coding agent, but nothing actually forces the agent to follow it. The tests it writes usually check what it built, rather than what you asked for. PDD Kit makes the agent keep the plan. It works with you to turn your intent into a formal specification in Verus (opens in new tab) , proves the agent’s code meets that spec for every input, and falls back to tests where a proof can’t reach. We tried it on a full-stack web app. Inside GitHub Next’s Chopin (opens in new tab) , we used PDD Kit to formally verify the login logic of Pet Store, a Rust (opens in new tab) storefront. Verus hardened the code and uncovered existing bugs, proving the absence of login bugs with respect to the specification. The developer reviewed the intent and never read the generated code line-by-line. The plan is the contract the agent should follow, but nothing constrains the agent to follow it. Coding agents now ship whole features in one sitting often spanning tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands of lines of code. As a result, reading every line of the pull request doesn’t scale to this new way of work. Now, most teams invest in the plan and relevant testing instead: describe to an agent what they want, go back and forth until the plan and proposed tests look right, and hand them off to the agent for implementation. This plan or natural language spec is meant to be the contract that an agent holds. However, in practice, the agent can drift from it. It implements something slightly different, then writes tests that pass for its implementation rather than the code you intended it to write. Continuous integration (CI) grows due to a profusion of low quality and high quantity of tests, coverage looks healthy, and the gap between what you asked for and what shipped stays hidden until a bug report or a nasty edge case shows up. So, how do you reliably scale review as agents generate increasingly large amounts of code? Agent code fails in two ways a careful reviewer would usually catch: it leaves out something obviously necessary, or it does something obviously wrong. Tests alone don’t close that gap, because they only exercise a tiny slice of what a program can do. Closing it needs a different kind of machinery, which is where proofs come in. PODCAST SERIES Ideas Listen as members of the research community at Microsoft discuss the beliefs that animate their research, the experiences and thinkers that inform it, and the positive human impact it targets. Listen now Opens in a new tab Review asks “does this look right?” A proof answers “is this right?” A mathematical proof shows that code meets its specification for every input, including the ones your test suite can miss. That provides stronger assurance for specified properties than testing alone, especially when line-by-line review isn’t practical. Proofs used to be too expensive for everyday software. You needed specialists, unfamiliar languages, proofs many times larger than the code, and proofs took years to develop, but two things have changed since. First, recent advances in coding agents have made it increasingly practical for them to help generate formal proofs from well-defined specs. Secondly, agents can now better help you write formal specs. We call this new software development paradigm Proof-Driven Development (PDD). PDD Kit is our toolkit for it. How PDD Kit works PDD Kit is to formal methods roughly what Spec Kit (opens in new tab) is to Spec-Driven Development. It runs as a partner inside Chopin (opens in new tab) , GitHub Next’s real-time, multiplayer planning environment, where a team and agents can plan in one shared document. The workflow has two halves (Figure 1). First, team members review intent in plain language. PDD Kit asks the questions a careful reviewer would ask, explains the relevant code as it goes, and records the answers in an intent artifact , a document that bridges the user’s intent with the formal specification or tests. The parts of the user’s intent that can be formalized are converted into formal specifications and the rest, which must be taken on trust, are converted to informal specifications for tests. PDD Kit automatically generates proofs that the code satisfies the derived formal specs and high-quality tests for the informal specs. You don’t need a formal methods background for any of it. Figure 1. Proof-Driven Development with PDD Kit. Team members settle intent. Verus and the test suite hold the code to it. Consequently, every result in PDD Kit says which kind of verification it rests on: Formal verification is a mathematical proof that code satisfies its specification for every possible input, checked by a tool called a verifier. For PDD Kit today, that verifier is Verus (opens in new tab) , a proof language for Rust co-developed by Microsoft Research, Carnegie Mellon University, VMware Research, ETH Zurich, MPI-SWS, UNSW Sydney, the University of Texas at Austin, the University of Michigan, the University of British Columbia, the University of Wisconsin–Madison and the Weizmann Institute of Science. Empirical verification checks code by running it and observing what it does. It covers what a proof can’t reach, such as a third-party cryptography library or a user interface. It uses unit and end-to-end tests, terminal automation, browser agents, and computer-use agents for anything a browser can’t drive. A passing test only shows the code worked on the inputs it tried, so PDD Kit labels it as evidence rather than proof. The line between the two is the Trusted Computing Base (TCB) : the code that the proof assumes behaves as described. PDD Kit makes that line explicit and asks you to sign off on each piece. The capstone: a full-stack web app To show PDD Kit integrating with existing codebases, we built Pet Store, a full-stack web app written entirely in Rust (opens in new tab) . The backend uses Axum (opens in new tab) and SQLite (opens in new tab) and handles inventory, promotions, orders and checkout. The storefront is a Leptos (opens in new tab) app compiled to WebAssembly (opens in new tab) . Together they come to about 5,000 lines of Rust. For brevity in this blog, we focus on formally verifying the login logic of the app, but the same process can be used to verify functional correctness of the entire app. PDD Kit recommends starting with the most sensitive parts of your application and incrementally verifying your application. A login bug can hand an attacker a customer’s account or an admin’s controls, so that’s where proof effort pays off first. The developer’s whole request in Chopin was two sentences: Verify the login logic in backend/src/handlers/auth.rs. Here are my requirements: You only get a token with the right password. Only admin accounts get admin tokens. We kept the request rough on purpose. Capturing the intent of the user and turning the user request into something a proof can check is PDD Kit’s job. Step 1: Questions before code PDD Kit’s planning workflow, pdd-plan, reads the code and comes back, before writing anything, with questions in a Decisions tab. When a question depends on how the code works, the card explains that part first: the goal, how the pieces fit, and the exact function involved, so you can answer without opening the source. Figure 2. The first decision card. “Only with the right password” on its own is also met by a login that refuses everyone. Proving both ways rules that out. The question looks pedantic, but it matters. “You only get a token with the right password” rules out the bad case, a wrong password getting a token, and a login that refuses everyone keeps that promise perfectly. “The right password always works” is the half that rules it out. Formally, the first is an implication (token ⇒ right password) and the second is its converse. Together they make an “if and only if.” An agent left alone would pick one without telling you, but here the developer picked both ways. Step 2: A human readable intent map As the conversation goes on, PDD Kit keeps a rough work section at the top of the plan current, so a user can keep track of important concepts without having to scroll back through a long chat to find what was agreed. It includes a flowchart of the login being specified, a spec landscape of what will be proved and what will be trusted, and, when a picture helps, a mental model. For login, PDD Kit drew a ticket desk (Figure 3). Figure 3. PDD Kit’s mental model for login. The field you send picks the window, the window picks the table and with it the role, and nothing prints until the password matches. Below it, the intent map ties each requirement back to the developer’s own words and records how it was settled (Figure 4). Each entry links to the section of the formal spec that models it and to the tests that cover it, and the spec section shows snippets of the Verus contract, annotated so the developer can see how the formal spec models their intent. Figure 4. An intent map entry after the decision: a login gets a token only with the right password for that account, and always with it. The flowchart shows every way the password check can end. The decision card in Figure 2 is the kind of ambiguity an agent would otherwise settle silently. Figure 5 shows how small the difference looks on paper: the two readings disagree in a single cell, a right password that gets no token. Figure 5. Two readings of the same sentence. They differ in one cell, and that cell changes what the proof has to establish. Step 3: Proving the login function Before anything gets built, PDD Kit asks the team to sign off on the plan as a whole. Its first draft proved the decision at the center of login, picking the table and gating on the password, and kept the handler around it trusted and tested. That’s a sensible default, and it’s what PDD Kit recommended, but the developer wanted more. The handler is where the lookups get awaited and the token gets signed, and that glue is exactly where a refactor can quietly swap two lines. So at intent review the developer chose to give the login handler its own async spec, so the proof covers that glue too instead of trusting it (Figure 6). Figure 6. Proving more of login means trusting more small wrappers. The card says so before the developer chooses. That choice moved almost everything into the proof and left the login handler with nothing to do but unpack the request. A new async function, login_flow , carries the contract from the request’s fields all the way to the token or the HTTP error. PDD Kit then brought the revised plan back for a fresh sign-off, because matching your intent isn’t proof, and it doesn’t approve new trust or a wider scope. Step 4: Where proof stops There are plenty of things you can’t prove about a program, and login runs into most of them: Code the verifier can’t see. bcrypt’s hashing, sqlx’s queries and jsonwebtoken’s signing live in other crates, outside the proof. Facts about the outside world. What SQLite holds right now and what time the clock says are inputs to the program, not something its code can establish. Whether, and how fast, something finishes. The spec says what you get if login answers. A hung query, or a slow one, breaks nothing in it. Anything a person has to judge , like whether an error message helps or a screen makes sense. Whatever nobody wrote down. A proof covers its spec and says nothing about requirements outside it. That’s where empirical verification comes in. PDD Kit spells out the trusted boundary, the part of the TCB this proof leans on. It wraps each trusted piece in a small function with an assumed contract, using Verus’s #[verifier::external_body] or external_fn_specification , asks the developer to accept each one on its own, and writes a test for every assumed clause into the plan. For login, the developer signed off on six pieces: The two lookups, Customer::find_by_email and Admin::find_by_username . Each awaited, successful lookup returns exactly the row its own table holds for that email or username, or none. check_password , a thin wrapper around bcrypt::verify . It errors only on a stored hash bcrypt can’t read, and Ok(true) means exactly the right password. generate_token , which signs exactly the claims it is given under the configured secret and reports a signing failure as a 500. expiry_from_now , which reads the clock and writes an expiry exactly 24 hours later. database_error , which turns a failed lookup into today’s 500 with sqlx’s message. The login handler shell, which unpacks the request and passes its fields to login_flow unchanged. In the spec, a lookup keeps its code where it is and gets a contract from the outside with external_fn_specification : /// Looks up a customer by exact email. /// Trusted, not proved: the SQL query runs in sqlx, which Verus cannot check. /// Every customer promise of `login_flow` rests on it. #[verifier::external_fn_specification] pub async fn ex_customer_find_by_email(pool: &sqlx::SqlitePool, email: &str) -> (r: Result , sqlx::Error>) ensures // When the query succeeds, it returns the customers row on // file for exactly this email, or None when there is none. r matches Ok(found) ==> found == customer_on_file(email@), { Customer::find_by_email(pool, email).await } The clock is a small wrapper marked #[verifier::external_body] . Verus uses its ensures clause and never reads the body: /// Reads the clock and computes a token's expiry 24 hours ahead. /// Trusted, not proved: chrono's clock is outside the proof. /// It panics if the time is out of range, as today's login does; /// that panic is not promised against. #[verifier::external_body] pub fn expiry_from_now() -> (r: Expiry) ensures // The expiry is exactly 24 hours (86,400 seconds) after the clock reading. r.exp as int == r.now as int + 86_400, { ... } Figure 7 puts the three layers together: what Verus proves, what people accept and tests check, and what nobody is promising. Figure 7. Where the login proof stops. Verus proves the core for every input. People accept the trusted ring and tests check it. The plan lists what nobody is promising. Figure 8 maps what gets proved and what gets trusted. Each trust decision is its own card. It shows the clauses Verus will take on faith, what the developer is accepting, and which promise falls apart if the assumption is wrong (Figure 9). Every assumed clause then gets an empirical check in the plan’s Empirical verification section, written as Given/When/Then scenarios before any test exists (Figure 10). An entry says planned until it has run, and then it records the command’s result and the commit it ran against. Figure 8. What gets proved and what gets trusted in login. Green functions are proved by Verus for every input. Amber pieces are trusted, accepted by the developer, and checked by the planned tests in the plan’s §4.1. Figure 9. A trust card for check_password . Verus takes these two clauses on faith, so a person accepts them and two tests check them. Figure 10. A planned test for the trusted check_password , written before the test exists. The plan labels a passing test as evidence rather than proof. The plan is just as explicit about what nobody is promising: that the login future ever completes, that an out-of-range clock won’t panic, anything about the timing or rate of attempts, and how other endpoints read the role. Step 5: Reading the spec The intent artifact is what the team reviews. It’s the plain-language version of the formal spec PDD Kit writes as Verus contracts. You might be wondering whether someone now has to read the proof instead of the code. Nobody does, because the coding agent writes the proof and Verus checks every step of it. If Verus accepts the proof, it holds whether or not anyone reads it. The spec is what the proof is held to, so that’s what people review, and this one is short enough to learn to read in a few minutes. Each function gets an ensures block: statements about its result, r, that must hold for every possible input. Verus checks them when you build, and if any clause could fail for even one input, the build fails and Verus points at that clause. Each clause reads as an if-then, and Figure 11 takes apart the clause for the developer’s first requirement. Figure 11. The ensures clause on login_flow for “You only get a token with the right password.” The same account a appears on every line, which ties the password check to the token. Notice that the same a appears on every line, which ties the password check to the token. For example, imagine a bug where login checks the password against one account but signs the token for another. Bob logs in with his own, correct password and gets back a token for Alice’s account. Each step looks fine on its own, but this clause catches it, because the password check and the token have to name the same account. That’s the kind of wiring bug a test suite rarely thinks to look for. The spec also has to talk about SQLite, bcrypt and JWTs without running any of them. It does that with uninterpreted functions , names with no body: customer_on_file(email) and admin_on_file(username) for the rows the database holds, bcrypt_verdict(password, hash) for what bcrypt would say, and token_claims(token, secret) for what a token carries. Verus knows nothing about them except what the trusted contracts from Step 4 promise. The proof says “whatever the database holds, login does the right thing with it,” and a trusted contract says “the lookup returns what the database holds.” /// The customers row the database holds for /// exactly this email, if any, when login looks. /// Left abstract: only `Customer::find_by_email`'s /// trusted contract says what it is. pub uninterp spec fn customer_on_file(email: Seq ) -> Option ; ... /// What bcrypt says about `password` against a /// stored `hash`: Some(true) when it is the password /// the hash was made from, Some(false) when it is /// not, None when bcrypt cannot read the hash. /// Left abstract: its meaning is bcrypt's, taken on trust through `check_password`. pub uninterp spec fn bcrypt_verdict(password: Seq , hash: Seq ) -> Option ; /// The password is the right one for the stored hash, by bcrypt's verdict. pub open spec fn password_matches(password: Seq , hash: Seq ) -> bool { bcrypt_verdict(password, hash) == Some(true) } On top of those, named_account(email, username) says which account a login names: the customers row for the email when one is sent, otherwise the admins row for the username, otherwise none. It’s written like Rust, but it’s a mathematical definition that never runs and only appears in contracts. Code like this is called ghost code , since the verifier checks it but the compiler erases it from the program. With it, the developer’s two-sentence request ends up as eight ensures clauses on login_flow (Figure 12). /// The account a login names: the customers row for /// the email when one is sent (role "customer"), /// otherwise the admins row for the username (role "admin"), otherwise none. pub open spec fn named_account(email: Option , username: Option ) -> Option { match email { Some(e) => match customer_on_file(e@) { Some(c) => Some(NamedAccount { id: c.id@, password_hash: c.password_hash@, role: customer_role() }), None => None, }, None => match username { Some(u) => match admin_on_file(u@) { Some(a) => Some(NamedAccount { id: a.id@, password_hash: a.password_hash@, role: admin_role() }), None => None, }, None => None, }, } } Figure 12. The two-sentence request and the Both ways decision ended up as eight ensures clauses on login_flow. Four of them keep today’s refusals, so the storefront and the existing API tests keep working. Here’s the whole contract, with its doc comment trimmed. Each clause has the plain-English comment above it that the intent artifact shows the team: /// The whole login, awaited end to end: from the /// request's fields to the token or the HTTP error. /// ... pub async fn login_flow(pool: &sqlx::SqlitePool, config: &Config, email: Option , username: Option , password: &str) -> (r: Result ) ensures // Neither an email nor a username: 400 with today's message. email is None && username is None ==> (r matches Err(AppError::BadRequest(m)) && m@ == missing_identity_text()), // A token only for the account the login names, with its right // password; it carries that account's id and its table's role. r matches Ok(t) ==> (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a) && password_matches(password@, a.password_hash) && token_claims(t@, config.jwt_secret@) matches Some(c) && c.sub@ == a.id && c.role@ == a.role), // The right password for the named account always gets a // token, unless a lookup or signing failure gives 500. (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a) && password_matches(password@, a.password_hash)) ==> (r is Ok || r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_))), // A login naming an account nobody holds gets // 401, unless the lookup fails with 500. ((email is Some || username is Some) && named_account(email, username) is None) ==> (r matches Err(AppError::Unauthorized) || r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_))), // A wrong password for an account whose hash bcrypt // can read gets 401, unless the lookup fails with 500. (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a) && bcrypt_verdict(password@, a.password_hash) == Some(false)) ==> (r matches Err(AppError::Unauthorized) || r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_))), // An account whose stored hash bcrypt cannot read gets 500 and no token. (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a) && bcrypt_verdict(password@, a.password_hash) is None) ==> r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_)), // The admin role only for an admins row // found by username, with no email sent. (r matches Ok(t) && token_claims(t@, config.jwt_secret@) matches Some(c) && c.role@ == admin_role()) ==> (email is None && username matches Some(u) && admin_on_file(u@) is Some), // An email login's token always carries the customer role. (r matches Ok(t) && email is Some) ==> (token_claims(t@, config.jwt_secret@) matches Some(c) && c.role@ == customer_role()), { unimplemented!() } The trusted boundary shows up in the code too. check_password is one of the functions whose body Verus doesn’t check. Its contract ties it to bcrypt_verdict , an uninterpreted model of bcrypt with no axioms: /// Asks bcrypt whether `password` matches the stored `hash`. /// Trusted, not proved: Verus cannot check bcrypt's hashing, /// so this wrapper's contract is assumed. /// Every password promise of `login_flow` rests on it. #[verifier::external_body] pub fn check_password(password: &str, hash: &str) -> (r: Result ) ensures // bcrypt answers (Ok) exactly when it can read the stored hash. r is Ok <==> bcrypt_verdict(password@, hash@) is Some, // Its answer is its verdict: true for the // right password, false for any other. r matches Ok(b) ==> bcrypt_verdict(password@, hash@) == Some(b), { bcrypt::verify(password, hash).map_err(|e| e.to_string()) } The doc comment above it says what rests on it: every password promise of login_flow . Every login ends in one of a handful of places, and only one of them has a token (Figure 13). The proof covers all of them at once. Figure 13. Every way a login can end, from the plan. login_flow is async: it awaits a database query. Verus can put contracts on async functions, with one rule worth knowing (Figure 14). requires is checked when the call creates the future. ensures describes

Below it, the intent map ties each requirement back to the developer’s own words and records how it was settled (Figure 4). Each entry links to the section of the formal spec that models it and to the tests that cover it, and the spec section shows snippets of the Verus contract, annotated so the developer can see how the formal spec models their intent. Figure 4. An intent map entry after the decision: a login gets a token only with the right password for that account, and always with it. The flowchart shows every way the password check can end. The decision card in Figure 2 is the kind of ambiguity an agent would otherwise settle silently. Figure 5 shows how small the difference looks on paper: the two readings disagree in a single cell, a right password that gets no token. Figure 5. Two readings of the same sentence. They differ in one cell, and that cell changes what the proof has to establish. Step 3: Proving the login function Before anything gets built, PDD Kit asks the team to sign off on the plan as a whole. Its first draft proved the decision at the center of login, picking the table and gating on the password, and kept the handler around it trusted and tested. That’s a sensible default, and it’s what PDD Kit recommended, but the developer wanted more. The handler is where the lookups get awaited and the token gets signed, and that glue is exactly where a refactor can quietly swap two lines. So at intent review the developer chose to give the login handler its own async spec, so the proof covers that glue too instead of trusting it (Figure 6). Figure 6. Proving more of login means trusting more small wrappers. The card says so before the developer chooses. That choice moved almost everything into the proof and left the login handler with nothing to do but unpack the request. A new async function, login_flow , carries the contract from the request’s fields all the way to the token or the HTTP error. PDD Kit then brought the revised plan back for a fresh sign-off, because matching your intent isn’t proof, and it doesn’t approve new trust or a wider scope. Step 4: Where proof stops There are plenty of things you can’t prove about a program, and login runs into most of them: Code the verifier can’t see. bcrypt’s hashing, sqlx’s queries and jsonwebtoken’s signing live in other crates, outside the proof. Facts about the outside world. What SQLite holds right now and what time the clock says are inputs to the program, not something its code can establish. Whether, and how fast, something finishes. The spec says what you get if login answers. A hung query, or a slow one, breaks nothing in it. Anything a person has to judge , like whether an error message helps or a screen makes sense. Whatever nobody wrote down. A proof covers its spec and says nothing about requirements outside it. That’s where empirical verification comes in. PDD Kit spells out the trusted boundary, the part of the TCB this proof leans on. It wraps each trusted piece in a small function with an assumed contract, using Verus’s #[verifier::external_body] or external_fn_specification , asks the developer to accept each one on its own, and writes a test for every assumed clause into the plan. For login, the developer signed off on six pieces: The two lookups, Customer::find_by_email and Admin::find_by_username . Each awaited, successful lookup returns exactly the row its own table holds for that email or username, or none. check_password , a thin wrapper around bcrypt::verify . It errors only on a stored hash bcrypt can’t read, and Ok(true) means exactly the right password. generate_token , which signs exactly the claims it is given under the configured secret and reports a signing failure as a 500. expiry_from_now , which reads the clock and writes an expiry exactly 24 hours later. database_error , which turns a failed lookup into today’s 500 with sqlx’s message. The login handler shell, which unpacks the request and passes its fields to login_flow unchanged. In the spec, a lookup keeps its code where it is and gets a contract from the outside with external_fn_specification : /// Looks up a customer by exact email. /// Trusted, not proved: the SQL query runs in sqlx, which Verus cannot check. /// Every customer promise of `login_flow` rests on it. #[verifier::external_fn_specification] pub async fn ex_customer_find_by_email(pool: &sqlx::SqlitePool, email: &str) -> (r: Result , sqlx::Error>) ensures // When the query succeeds, it returns the customers row on // file for exactly this email, or None when there is none. r matches Ok(found) ==> found == customer_on_file(email@), { Customer::find_by_email(pool, email).await } The clock is a small wrapper marked #[verifier::external_body] . Verus uses its ensures clause and never reads the body: /// Reads the clock and computes a token's expiry 24 hours ahead. /// Trusted, not proved: chrono's clock is outside the proof. /// It panics if the time is out of range, as today's login does; /// that panic is not promised against. #[verifier::external_body] pub fn expiry_from_now() -> (r: Expiry) ensures // The expiry is exactly 24 hours (86,400 seconds) after the clock reading. r.exp as int == r.now as int + 86_400, { ... } Figure 7 puts the three layers together: what Verus proves, what people accept and tests check, and what nobody is promising. Figure 7. Where the login proof stops. Verus proves the core for every input. People accept the trusted ring and tests check it. The plan lists what nobody is promising. Figure 8 maps what gets proved and what gets trusted. Each trust decision is its own card. It shows the clauses Verus will take on faith, what the developer is accepting, and which promise falls apart if the assumption is wrong (Figure 9). Every assumed clause then gets an empirical check in the plan’s Empirical verification section, written as Given/When/Then scenarios before any test exists (Figure 10). An entry says planned until it has run, and then it records the command’s result and the commit it ran against. Figure 8. What gets proved and what gets trusted in login. Green functions are proved by Verus for every input. Amber pieces are trusted, accepted by the developer, and checked by the planned tests in the plan’s §4.1. Figure 9. A trust card for check_password . Verus takes these two clauses on faith, so a person accepts them and two tests check them. Figure 10. A planned test for the trusted check_password , written before the test exists. The plan labels a passing test as evidence rather than proof. The plan is just as explicit about what nobody is promising: that the login future ever completes, that an out-of-range clock won’t panic, anything about the timing or rate of attempts, and how other endpoints read the role. Step 5: Reading the spec The intent artifact is what the team reviews. It’s the plain-language version of the formal spec PDD Kit writes as Verus contracts. You might be wondering whether someone now has to read the proof instead of the code. Nobody does, because the coding agent writes the proof and Verus checks every step of it. If Verus accepts the proof, it holds whether or not anyone reads it. The spec is what the proof is held to, so that’s what people review, and this one is short enough to learn to read in a few minutes. Each function gets an ensures block: statements about its result, r, that must hold for every possible input. Verus checks them when you build, and if any clause could fail for even one input, the build fails and Verus points at that clause. Each clause reads as an if-then, and Figure 11 takes apart the clause for the developer’s first requirement. Figure 11. The ensures clause on login_flow for “You only get a token with the right password.” The same account a appears on every line, which ties the password check to the token. Notice that the same a appears on every line, which ties the password check to the token. For example, imagine a bug where login checks the password against one account but signs the token for another. Bob logs in with his own, correct password and gets back a token for Alice’s account. Each step looks fine on its own, but this clause catches it, because the password check and the token have to name the same account. That’s the kind of wiring bug a test suite rarely thinks to look for. The spec also has to talk about SQLite, bcrypt and JWTs without running any of them. It does that with uninterpreted functions , names with no body: customer_on_file(email) and admin_on_file(username) for the rows the database holds, bcrypt_verdict(password, hash) for what bcrypt would say, and token_claims(token, secret) for what a token carries. Verus knows nothing about them except what the trusted contracts from Step 4 promise. The proof says “whatever the database holds, login does the right thing with it,” and a trusted contract says “the lookup returns what the database holds.” /// The customers row the database holds for /// exactly this email, if any, when login looks. /// Left abstract: only `Customer::find_by_email`'s /// trusted contract says what it is. pub uninterp spec fn customer_on_file(email: Seq ) -> Option ; ... /// What bcrypt says about `password` against a /// stored `hash`: Some(true) when it is the password /// the hash was made from, Some(false) when it is /// not, None when bcrypt cannot read the hash. /// Left abstract: its meaning is bcrypt's, taken on trust through `check_password`. pub uninterp spec fn bcrypt_verdict(password: Seq , hash: Seq ) -> Option ; /// The password is the right one for the stored hash, by bcrypt's verdict. pub open spec fn password_matches(password: Seq , hash: Seq ) -> bool { bcrypt_verdict(password, hash) == Some(true) } On top of those, named_account(email, username) says which account a login names: the customers row for the email when one is sent, otherwise the admins row for the username, otherwise none. It’s written like Rust, but it’s a mathematical definition that never runs and only appears in contracts. Code like this is called ghost code , since the verifier checks it but the compiler erases it from the program. With it, the developer’s two-sentence request ends up as eight ensures clauses on login_flow (Figure 12). /// The account a login names: the customers row for /// the email when one is sent (role "customer"), /// otherwise the admins row for the username (role "admin"), otherwise none. pub open spec fn named_account(email: Option , username: Option ) -> Option { match email { Some(e) => match customer_on_file(e@) { Some(c) => Some(NamedAccount { id: c.id@, password_hash: c.password_hash@, role: customer_role() }), None => None, }, None => match username { Some(u) => match admin_on_file(u@) { Some(a) => Some(NamedAccount { id: a.id@, password_hash: a.password_hash@, role: admin_role() }), None => None, }, None => None, }, } } Figure 12. The two-sentence request and the Both ways decision ended up as eight ensures clauses on login_flow. Four of them keep today’s refusals, so the storefront and the existing API tests keep working. Here’s the whole contract, with its doc comment trimmed. Each clause has the plain-English comment above it that the intent artifact shows the team: /// The whole login, awaited end to end: from the /// request's fields to the token or the HTTP error. /// ... pub async fn login_flow(pool: &sqlx::SqlitePool, config: &Config, email: Option , username: Option , password: &str) -> (r: Result ) ensures // Neither an email nor a username: 400 with today's message. email is None && username is None ==> (r matches Err(AppError::BadRequest(m)) && m@ == missing_identity_text()), // A token only for the account the login names, with its right // password; it carries that account's id and its table's role. r matches Ok(t) ==> (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a) && password_matches(password@, a.password_hash) && token_claims(t@, config.jwt_secret@) matches Some(c) && c.sub@ == a.id && c.role@ == a.role), // The right password for the named account always gets a // token, unless a lookup or signing failure gives 500. (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a) && password_matches(password@, a.password_hash)) ==> (r is Ok || r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_))), // A login naming an account nobody holds gets // 401, unless the lookup fails with 500. ((email is Some || username is Some) && named_account(email, username) is None) ==> (r matches Err(AppError::Unauthorized) || r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_))), // A wrong password for an account whose hash bcrypt // can read gets 401, unless the lookup fails with 500. (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a) && bcrypt_verdict(password@, a.password_hash) == Some(false)) ==> (r matches Err(AppError::Unauthorized) || r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_))), // An account whose stored hash bcrypt cannot read gets 500 and no token. (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a) && bcrypt_verdict(password@, a.password_hash) is None) ==> r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_)), // The admin role only for an admins row // found by username, with no email sent. (r matches Ok(t) && token_claims(t@, config.jwt_secret@) matches Some(c) && c.role@ == admin_role()) ==> (email is None && username matches Some(u) && admin_on_file(u@) is Some), // An email login's token always carries the customer role. (r matches Ok(t) && email is Some) ==> (token_claims(t@, config.jwt_secret@) matches Some(c) && c.role@ == customer_role()), { unimplemented!() } The trusted boundary shows up in the code too. check_password is one of the functions whose body Verus doesn’t check. Its contract ties it to bcrypt_verdict , an uninterpreted model of bcrypt with no axioms: /// Asks bcrypt whether `password` matches the stored `hash`. /// Trusted, not proved: Verus cannot check bcrypt's hashing, /// so this wrapper's contract is assumed. /// Every password promise of `login_flow` rests on it. #[verifier::external_body] pub fn check_password(password: &str, hash: &str) -> (r: Result ) ensures // bcrypt answers (Ok) exactly when it can read the stored hash. r is Ok <==> bcrypt_verdict(password@, hash@) is Some, // Its answer is its verdict: true for the // right password, false for any other. r matches Ok(b) ==> bcrypt_verdict(password@, hash@) == Some(b), { bcrypt::verify(password, hash).map_err(|e| e.to_string()) } The doc comment above it says what rests on it: every password promise of login_flow . Every login ends in one of a handful of places, and only one of them has a token (Figure 13). The proof covers all of them at once. Figure 13. Every way a login can end, from the plan. login_flow is async: it awaits a database query. Verus can put contracts on async functions, with one rule worth knowing (Figure 14). requires is checked when the call creates the future. ensures describes

items.summary: Make america healthy again President Trump launched the Make America Healthy Again initiative to confront chronic disease, improve nutrition, and lower healthcare costs. This year, the administration advanced reforms targeting childhood health, food quality, and preventive care while increasing transparency and accountability in healthcare systems. These actions are laying the foundation for a healthier, stronger America. By prioritizing prevention over treatment and empowering families with better information and choices, the administration is addressing the root causes of poor health outcomes. These efforts are improving quality of life, strengthening communities, and ensuring a healthier future for the next generation of Americans. items.content: At a glance A new form of computing . Zero-knowledge proofs let you run a workload and receive, alongside the result, a short proof that the program ran correctly. Anyone can check the proof in milliseconds, without rerunning the program, without trusting whoever ran it, and without needing data on which the program was run. Three grand challenges have stood in the way of broad adoption : making proofs fast enough to produce, making them available to normal programs without cryptographic expertise, and resting them on cryptography that will still be trusted many decades from now. Magnetar makes major progress on all three challenges. It proves programs written in Rust, Go, or C, runs 10 to 39 times faster on average than the prior fastest comparable systems, and rests its security only on standard hash functions. It is the latest result of more than a decade of research at Microsoft Research on making zero-knowledge proofs practical. A new form of computing Every result a computer produces comes with an implicit question: did the program run as claimed and produce correct outputs? Today, answering that question often requires a degree of trust alongside verification. We trust the operator, the vendor, the counterparty, or the agent, and we rely on contracts, audits, and logs to establish that trust. Zero-knowledge proofs offer a fundamentally different approach to establishing trust. A program runs, and along with its output it produces a short proof, a cryptographic certificate that this program, on these inputs, produced this output. The proof is small and fast to check. Whoever receives it can confirm the result in milliseconds without rerunning the program, and can pass the proof on to anyone else who needs the same assurance. With the zero-knowledge property, the proof also reveals nothing about inputs that should stay private. This changes what correctness means in the real world. A result no longer has to be trusted because of who produced it. It can be checked because of what accompanies it. An AI agent acting on someone’s behalf could attach a proof that each action complied with the policy it was given. Regulated financial institutions could prove that transactions were processed correctly without making their transactions public. These become possible once producing a proof is as routine as running the program. Three grand challenges Zero-knowledge proofs were invented in the 1980s, and the ideas behind proving program execution have been around nearly as long. What has kept them from becoming a general tool is three challenges that have resisted being solved at the same time. Efficiency . Producing a proof has historically taken millions of times more computation than running the program itself. Years of research have brought that overhead down, but the fastest systems have achieved their speed by making compromises elsewhere. Generality and usability. Many proof systems require developers to manually rewrite their program as a cryptographic circuit, which is a fixed arithmetic description of that exact computation. This takes months. Every change to the application means a new circuit, and the translation is itself a frequent source of security bugs. A general-purpose alternative is to prove the execution of an ordinary processor, so that any compiled program can be proven as written. Until recently, that generality came at a steep cost in speed or security. Security. A proof is only as strong as the cryptography beneath it. Many proof systems rest on elliptic curves, which can be broken by a sufficiently powerful quantum computer. Microsoft is addressing this problem with its Quantum Safe Program, which will move its products and services to post-quantum cryptography, a goal it recently accelerated to 2029 . Post-quantum proof systems already exist, but some rest on lattice assumptions, and most rest on new cryptographic functions invented to reduce the cost of proving. These new cryptographic functions have not faced the decades of scrutiny given to the cryptography protecting today’s internet, and some rest on mathematical conjectures about error-correcting codes that have not been proven. They have bought their speed with strong assumptions. PODCAST SERIES The Shape of Things to Come Join Microsoft’s Doug Burger and guests as they dig into the fundamental truths about AI and how it will reshape the future. Listen now Opens in a new tab More than a decade of work For more than a decade, Microsoft Research has worked on making zero-knowledge proofs and verifiable computing practical. Early research followed two approaches, both practical only for small programs. The first (opens in new tab) (opens in new tab) lets a verifier check a long computation through a short conversation with the prover using a technique called the sum-check protocol (opens in new tab) , but this applied only to computations with a particular layered structure. The second (opens in new tab) (opens in new tab) used elliptic-curve cryptography to create very small proofs for almost any computation. But this requires a one-time trusted setup involving secret information which, if leaked, could allow anyone to forge proofs. This approach is also vulnerable to quantum computers. In 2019, a new zero-knowledge proof system called Spartan returned to the sum-check approach and made it work for general-purpose programs without a trusted setup. Spartan can also be instantiated with different cryptographic building blocks. That flexibility is what later allowed the proof system to be built on hash functions alone. A sequence of results then filled in the remaining pieces: Phalanx (opens in new tab) , in 2021, showed how to exploit repetition, such as a processor running the same instruction cycle on every step, to prove computations an order of magnitude faster than Spartan. Magnetar’s processor description is built on this idea. Nova (opens in new tab) , HyperNova (opens in new tab) , NeutronNova (opens in new tab) , Neo and SuperNeo (opens in new tab) showed that stopping Spartan’s proving early, and folding the partial results together, makes it practical to prove computations of any size at far lower cost. Brakedown (opens in new tab) , in 2021, introduced a fast hash-based commitment scheme and combined it with Spartan, giving the first Spartan variant whose security rests on standard hash functions. Spice (opens in new tab) , Lasso (opens in new tab) , Nebula (opens in new tab) , and then Twist and Shout (opens in new tab) made the memory operations at the heart of a general-purpose processor inexpensive to prove, and Jolt (opens in new tab) showed that combining them with Spartan can efficiently prove the execution of a complete processor. Earlier this year, Vega (opens in new tab) applied this line of work to digital identity, proving facts from a government credential in under a tenth of a second . More recently, BinarySpartan (opens in new tab) brought Spartan to binary fields, where a processor’s logic and standard hash functions can be efficiently expressed. BinarySpartan also relies on Ligerito (opens in new tab) , a Brakedown-style commitment scheme with much shorter proofs, and on ring switching (opens in new tab) , which makes it efficient to commit to vectors of bits. Each of these solved a piece of the problem. Magnetar is where the pieces come together. Magnetar Magnetar is a zero-knowledge virtual machine, or zkVM, and it makes major progress on all three challenges at once. Figure 1. Magnetar proves a program’s execution and returns a small proof that anyone can check, with security resting only on standard hash functions. It is general-purpose. Magnetar proves the execution of RISC-V, an open processor architecture with mature compilers for every mainstream language. A developer writes a program in Rust, Go, or C, compiles it as usual, and Magnetar proves it as written. Consider what this means in practice. A business policy, a data pipeline, or an interpreter for the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) is just a program, and the engineers who already maintain it can prove their executions exactly as written. As a result, proving stops being a specialist activity. It is faster than prior systems in the same class. Magnetar proves 7.2 to 8.7 million processor instructions per second on a laptop. Across 15 benchmark programs, from cryptographic hashing to token transfers inside a small EVM interpreter, it is 10 to 39 times faster on average than the fastest existing zkVMs on the same machine, and more than 300 times faster than two others on a token-transfer benchmark. An optimized Magnetar proves 9.5–12.8 million cycles per second, which increases each speedup reported here by about 1.3×. Its proofs verify in about 12 milliseconds. Its security rests on standard cryptography. Magnetar depends on a standard hash function such as SHA-256 or SHA-3, the same primitives that already protect every organization’s systems. It requires no elliptic curves, no lattices, no special-purpose hash functions, no trusted setup, and no unproven conjecture about error-correcting codes. Hash functions are the most thoroughly studied primitives in the cryptographic toolkit, and they are the basis of the stateless hash-based signatures that NIST standardized as its own conservative post-quantum option. For a system that must still be trustworthy in many decades to come, relying only on standard hash functions removes a cryptographic migration from the roadmap. The same design decision pays a second dividend. Checking a Magnetar proof consists mostly of evaluating standard hash functions and binary-field arithmetic, which are exactly the operations Magnetar proves efficiently. Verifying a proof is therefore an ordinary workload for it. This is what allows Magnetar to prove computations of any size, by proving them in pieces and then combining the pieces. This also allows Magnetar to prove a long-running system such as a ledger or a blockchain. The technical paper gives the full design, security analysis, and measurements. Looking ahead Magnetar advances zero-knowledge proofs and verifiable computing to a stage where they can be built on the cryptography that organizations already trust, at speeds that make it usable, by engineers who write normal code. Magnetar enables a future where cryptographic proofs are a routine output of computation. We expect that technology leaders will stop asking whether proofs of execution are practical and focus instead on which results would they prefer to verify rather than taking on trust . If you’re interested in exploring how zero-knowledge proofs can support your use case, we’d love to hear from you (opens in new tab) . items.title: Solving a 31-year-old grand challenge in mathematics – the KLS conjecture

items.content: Microsoft researcher and collaborator combine new mathematical ideas with human-directed AI to resolve a central problem in high-dimensional geometry and probability At a glance Fundamental scientific breakthrough: Researchers resolved the Kannan-Lovász-Simonovits (KLS) conjecture, a 31-year-old problem widely regarded as one of the central open questions in high-dimensional geometry, with implications for statistics, optimization, algorithms, and computer science. A universal geometric principle: The result establishes a universal geometric principle for log-concave distributions, showing that simple flat cuts can capture their narrowest bottlenecks within a fixed factor, regardless of dimension. Human-AI collaboration: The breakthrough emerged from a human-directed agentic research process in which AI systems explored mathematical possibilities while researchers evaluated, pruned, and redirected the search. Independent confirmation: Multiple independent researchers have validated this research, identifying its central criterion as the key breakthrough, followed by a machine-checked formal verification. For decades, a fundamental question about the difficulty of computing in high-dimensional spaces has resisted proof. New research resolves this question, removing a major theoretical obstacle to understanding the efficiency of randomized algorithms used across science and computing. The Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits (KLS) conjecture was proposed in 1995. It asks whether, for a broad class of high-dimensional probability distributions, the best flat or hyperplane cut is always nearly as effective as the best cut of any shape. More precisely, KLS predicts that the two differ by no more than a universal constant, regardless of the number of dimensions. This would establish a dimension-free geometric principle with important consequences for high-dimensional geometry, probability, and theoretical computer science. Because the geometry of these cuts governs how quickly random walks can explore a distribution, KLS also plays a central role in the theory of high-dimensional sampling. Figure 1: An illustration of the KLS Conjecture (simplified) on regular tetrahedron. Since 1995, mathematicians have accumulated evidence that the conjecture was true, but a complete proof remained elusive. Now, two researchers, including Xinzhi Zhang from the Machine Learning and Optimization group at Microsoft Research, have proved the KLS conjecture (opens in new tab) . They have shown that the relationship holds with a fixed bound, regardless of how many dimensions a shape has. Before this work, the best known result (opens in new tab) , established in July 2026, allowed that bound to grow slowly as the number of dimensions increased. This work establishes a fundamental geometric principle: high-dimensional spaces are better behaved than previously known, and the obstacles to navigating them do not grow without bound as dimensions increase. ACADEMIC CONFERENCE Microsoft at SOSP 2026 Academic and industrial participants present research and experience papers that cover the full range of theory and practice of computer systems software. Learn more Opens in a new tab The importance of the KLS conjecture was recognized across the field long before it was resolved. In its 2017-18 Annual Report, the Mathematical Sciences Research Institute (MSRI) (opens in new tab) called it “a central open problem in high-dimensional convex geometry.” The Simons Institute (opens in new tab) described it as “one of the most important open problems in convex geometry.” In the proceedings of the 2022 International Congress of Mathematicians (ICM) (opens in new tab) , Ronen Eldan noted its broad implications for high-dimensional convex and computational geometry. Quanta Magazine (opens in new tab) wrote that KLS “lies at the heart of many questions in statistics and computer science.” Technical details The authors began by improving the July 2026 result in order to make the mathematical bound more precise. Working with AI agents in a structured, human-directed process, they explored more than 100 candidate approaches, many involving lengthy calculations with higher-order tensors. This produced a new mathematical criterion that became the foundation of the final proof. The authors then discovered that the new criterion could be applied recursively. Each improved bound could be fed back into the same argument to produce a still tighter one. In the October 1, 2026 version of the paper, this reduced the dependence on dimension to the iterated logarithm. This function grows extraordinarily slowly, but it still grows with the dimension and therefore did not yet fully resolve the conjecture. The final step was to repeat the entire recursive refinement, rather than applying it only once. This idea was inspired by the authors’ earlier work on fast algorithms for linear programming. The authors proved that the small errors introduced at each stage shrink fast enough that their total remains bounded by a universal constant, independent of the dimension. This eliminated the dependence on the number of dimensions and completed the proof in the October 4, 2026 version of the paper. The recursive method, its repeated application, and the proof that the accumulated errors remain bounded are original contributions of the researchers. AI tools helped explore candidate approaches, carry out detailed derivations, prepare the manuscript, and perform internal proof checks. The researchers determined the mathematical direction, selected the promising ideas, assembled them into the final argument, and verified the proof. Independent confirmation On the same day that the authors posted their complete proof, a separate group of leading experts posted a full proof (opens in new tab) that they developed in parallel. Their work built upon the findings in the first version (opens in new tab) of the Microsoft paper, calling it “the crucial step in the proof.” A third proof (opens in new tab) which appeared separately on the same day relies on a closely related idea. In addition, a Lean 4 formalization (opens in new tab) was subsequently released, combining the key criterion from the first Microsoft paper with additional research. Independent proofs are among mathematics’ strongest forms of validation because they demonstrate that a result does not rest on a single chain of reasoning. The subsequent appearance of alternative approaches and formal verification further strengthens confidence that the field has uncovered a genuine underlying principle rather than a fragile technical argument. The authors have also shortened their proof and verified the streamlined argument in Lean; they plan to release both after final review. Together, these developments provide complementary forms of confirmation. Human-AI guidance In the process of proving KLS, this research also demonstrates the power of having researchers direct AI rather than simply asking AI to solve a complex problem through a single end-to-end run of a frontier model or agent. The authors used an agentic search process with iterative, human-assisted “pruning”: As multiple agents explored variations of an idea in parallel, the researcher examined their intermediate result, eliminated unpromising directions, and passed the most promising result to the next round. Roughly one hundred research trajectories were explored before the key breakthrough emerged. In a separate track of the project, the authors made repeated unguided attempts to solve the same problem with several leading AI models, using roughly the same total token budget as the main process. That effort fell short of the goal. The eventual success depended on both the capabilities of the AI systems and the mathematical judgment of the researchers. Conclusion Taken together, resolving KLS settles a central problem in high-dimensional geometry. A wide range of results that previously relied on the conjecture as an assumption can now be stated unconditionally. The proof therefore provides a stronger foundation for research in convex geometry, probability, and theoretical computer science. The work also demonstrates how carefully guided human-AI collaboration can contribute to genuine scientific discovery while reinforcing, rather than replacing human insight. It highlights the continuing importance of scientific judgment in identifying promising directions, recognizing conceptual connections, and seeing when a partial insight points toward a deeper result. The authors are now simplifying the proof and extending its formal verification so that the mathematics and theoretical computer science communities can more easily examine the result and build on it. Acknowledgements Thank you to our co-author Zhao Song for his contributions to this work, and Victor Reis (opens in new tab) and Ishai Menache for helpful discussions throughout the project.
